items.title: Video of the Week: Water, Get Enemy? Directed by Daniel Obasi
items.content:
On the edge of Lagos, where the city meets the Atlantic, Water, Get Enemy? follows a community of young surfers who have grown up around the waters of Tarkwa Bay. Directed by Daniel Obasi, the short film looks beyond surfing as a sport to explore the relationships, routines and sense of freedom that have formed around it.

Through intimate testimonies and images moving between the ocean and the city beyond it, the film presents Tarkwa Bay as both an escape from the pressures of Lagos and a space for self-expression, friendship and belonging. For its surfers, the water is not simply somewhere to ride waves, but a place where an alternative way of living together has taken shape.

C41 spoke with Obasi about documenting this community, challenging established representations of surf culture, and the role of the ocean in shaping a different image of contemporary Lagos.

 

Gaia V. Marraffa: Surf culture has long been framed through a predominantly Eurocentric, Californian imaginary. Where does Water, Get Enemy? sit within your wider visual practice of repositioning West Africa as a centre of contemporary, hedonistic subcultures?

Daniel Obasi: Surf culture is often seen through a Western lens. With Water, Get Enemy?, I wanted to centre West Africa and show Lagos as a place with its own youth culture, freedom and pleasure.

GVM: Throughout the film, low-angle shots turn the young surfers into almost statuesque silhouettes against the skies of Tarkwa Bay. How did you develop this visual language, and what interested you in the relationship between their physicality, style and the particular grace of this community?

DO: I was drawn to their physicality and the way they move through the water. The low angles give them presence and scale while keeping their individuality and style visible.

GVM: Through the voice-overs, the ocean emerges as more than a playground: it becomes a place to decompress, away from the anxiety and depression that can accompany life in Lagos. What does the act of reclaiming mental wellbeing through nature mean to you, both personally and politically?

DO: For me, the ocean represents release. It offers a space away from Lagos’s noise and pressure, where you can reconnect with yourself, nature and others.

GVM: Some of the surfers speak about their families’ disapproval of the sport, while describing surfing itself as an essential expression of personal freedom. Do you see Lagos’s younger generation redefining ideas of priority, passion and self-fulfilment in relation to more traditional expectations?

DO: I think so. There’s a generation questioning what they’ve been told their lives should look like and making space for genuine happiness and fulfilment.

GVM: The film celebrates a remarkably close-knit collective, formed in and around the water. Against the intensity and complexity of Lagos, how important was it for you to portray the ocean as a place where intimacy, community and chosen families can take shape?

DO: That community was central to the film. I wanted the water to feel like a meeting point—a place where people could connect, build relationships and create a sense of family beyond traditional structures.

GVM: Beyond the waves, we catch glimpses of Lagos’s modern skyline and industrial coastline. How did you approach the visual and spatial tension between the creative isolation of Tarkwa Bay and the metropolis that surrounds it?

DO: I wanted that contrast to feel natural. Tarkwa Bay seems removed from Lagos, but the city is always visible in the distance. That tension became part of the film’s visual language.

GVM: Water, Get Enemy? captures a particular feeling of freedom and belonging. Do you see the film as a self-contained chapter in your exploration of youth identity in Lagos, or as part of a wider cinematic language you want to continue developing?

DO: It’s part of a wider exploration. I’m interested in young people, identity, freedom and the ways Lagos shapes how we see ourselves. I’d like to keep developing those ideas through film.

items.title_es: Video de la semana: ¿Agua, Enemigo? Dirigido por Daniel Obasi
items.content_es:
En el borde de Lagos, donde la ciudad se encuentra con el Atlántico, ¿Agua, enemiga? sigue a una comunidad de jóvenes surfistas que han crecido alrededor de las aguas de la bahía de Tarkwa. Dirigida por Daniel Obasi, el cortometraje se ve más allá del surf como un deporte para explorar las relaciones, rutinas y sentido de libertad que se han formado alrededor de ella.

A través de testimonios íntimos e imágenes que se mueven entre el océano y la ciudad más allá de él, la película presenta la Bahía de Tarkwa como un escape de las presiones de Lagos y un espacio para la autoexpresión, la amistad y la pertenencia. Para sus surfistas, el agua no es simplemente un lugar para montar olas, sino un lugar donde una forma alternativa de vivir juntos ha tomado forma.

C41 habló con Obasi sobre documentar esta comunidad, desafiando las representaciones establecidas de la cultura del surf, y el papel del océano en la configuración de una imagen diferente de Lagos contemporáneos.

 

Gaia V. Marraffa: La cultura del Surf se ha enmarcado durante mucho tiempo a través de un imaginario predominantemente eurocéntrico, californiano. ¿Dónde está el Agua, Obtener Enemigo? sentarse dentro de su práctica visual más amplia de reposicionar África Occidental como centro de subculturas hedonistas contemporáneas?

Daniel Obasi: La cultura del Surf se ve a menudo a través de una lente occidental. Con Agua, Get Enemy?, quería centrar África Occidental y mostrar Lagos como un lugar con su propia cultura juvenil, libertad y placer.

GVM: A lo largo de la película, las fotos de bajo ángulo convierten a los jóvenes surfistas en siluetas casi estatuas contra los cielos de la bahía de Tarkwa. ¿Cómo desarrollaste este lenguaje visual, y qué te interesaba en la relación entre su físico, estilo y la gracia particular de esta comunidad?

DO: Me atrajo a su fisicalidad y la forma en que se mueven a través del agua. Los ángulos bajos les dan presencia y escala manteniendo su individualidad y estilo visible.

GVM: A través de la voz-sobres, el océano emerge como más que un parque infantil: se convierte en un lugar para descomprimir, lejos de la ansiedad y depresión que puede acompañar la vida en Lagos. ¿Qué significa el acto de reclamar el bienestar mental a través de la naturaleza, tanto personal como políticamente?

DO: Para mí, el océano representa la liberación. Ofrece un espacio lejos del ruido y la presión de Lagos, donde se puede reconectar con usted mismo, la naturaleza y otros.

GVM: Algunos de los surfistas hablan de la desaprobación del deporte de sus familias, describiendo el surf como una expresión esencial de la libertad personal. ¿Ve usted a la generación más joven de Lagos redefiniendo ideas de prioridad, pasión y autocumplimiento en relación con expectativas más tradicionales?

DO: Creo que sí. Hay una generación cuestionando lo que se les ha dicho que sus vidas deben parecer y hacer espacio para la verdadera felicidad y realización.

GVM: La película celebra un colectivo notablemente cercano, formado en y alrededor del agua. Contra la intensidad y complejidad de Lagos, ¿qué tan importante era que retrataras el océano como un lugar donde la intimidad, la comunidad y las familias elegidas pueden tomar forma?

DO: Esa comunidad era central en la película. Quería que el agua se sintiera como un punto de encuentro, un lugar donde la gente pudiera conectar, construir relaciones y crear un sentido de familia más allá de las estructuras tradicionales.

GVM: Más allá de las olas, se observan los efectos del horizonte moderno y la costa industrial de Lagos. ¿Cómo se acercaron a la tensión visual y espacial entre el aislamiento creativo de la bahía de Tarkwa y la metrópolis que la rodea?

DO: Yo quería que el contraste se sintiera natural. Tarkwa Bay parece removida de Lagos, pero la ciudad es siempre visible a la distancia. Esa tensión se convirtió en parte del lenguaje visual de la película.

GVM: ¿Agua, Enemigo? captura una sensación particular de libertad y pertenencia. ¿Ves la película como un capítulo autocontenido en tu exploración de identidad juvenil en Lagos, o como parte de un lenguaje cinematográfico más amplio que desea seguir desarrollando?

DO: Es parte de una exploración más amplia. Me interesan los jóvenes, la identidad, la libertad y la forma en que Lagos forma cómo nos vemos. Me gustaría seguir desarrollando esas ideas a través del cine.

items.title: Salone Raritas: this is how it went
items.content:
Salone Raritas brought one-off and limited edition design pieces, antiques, and high craftsmanship to the trade fair for the first time this year.  The exhibitors Nina Yashar, Massimo Lunardon, Bruno Botticelli, and Francesco Faccin share their thoughts.

Salone Raritas. Curated icons, unique objects, and outsider pieces in Pavilion 9 move the spotlight on beauty, craftsmanship, and sustainability, amongst other things. Curated by  Annalisa Rosso, Editorial Director and Cultural Advisor to the Salone del Mobile.Milano, and with an exhibition display designed by Formafantasma, the platform showcased some of the most influential realities of the global scene, as well as some rare true gems. We asked some of the exhibitors to share their opinions while still fresh.  

Master glassblower Massimo Lunardon had this to say: ‘Salone Raritas was a new experience: refreshing, buzzy, and wonderful. Seen from inside, it was the jewel in the crown of the Salone del Mobile; a small event that, while showcasing antique objects and pieces from a more recent past, felt decidedly innovative and “young.” It was also extremely satisfying in terms of turnout, with lots of really interesting visits on the first day from people culturally prepared for what they were going to see, and a creditable press presence from all the leading newspapers. There was a different sort of public on the following days, but all very curious about what they were looking at.’ 

Bruno Botticelli, President of Associazione Antiquari d’Italia (Italian Antique Dealers Association), described Salone Raritas as an interesting experience with no shortage of proposals. ‘We certainly met a different sort of public, keen to find fresh inspiration, but I believe an educational element is needed to introduce a world that is unknown to most people, especially to non-Italians. Whilst people living in this country have a natural familiarity with the ancient world, Italy’s artistic and manufacturing heritage remains a closed book to many others around the globe. We are living in a time when there is a clear need for uniqueness in every aspect of our lives. This need is even stronger among the younger generations who, despite having partly moved on from their fixation with logos, need new keys for interpreting the concept of collectible objects that resonate with the new languages of design.’

Salone Raritas is therefore not just an exhibition space, but a diffusor of a new education in design. 

Nina Yashar, founder of Nilufar, also shared the same opinion, stating that ‘it was particularly significant to see an institution such as Salone del Mobile devote great attention to the world of collectible design and, more generally, to the concept of rarity. Not so much as a trend, rather as an attitude and a receptivity: a way of observing, selecting and connecting objects and visions.’

After all, Salone Raritas and Nilufar are not such different projects: ‘Nilufar stemmed precisely from this constant desire to explore what has not yet been fully told, affording space to different languages in dialogue with one another without hierarchies. At Raritas, I found this same openness and desire to create a space dedicated to research, experimentation, and vision.’

Lastly, she mentioned the importance of the visitors: ‘We were also pleasantly impressed by the quality and breadth of the public. There was an opportunity to engage with interior designers and industry professionals from diverse backgrounds, as well as key figures in the furnishings industry. This broad-based interest is, in my view, one of the most significant factors to emerge from this first edition, highlighting an increasing curiosity towards collectible design, and a greater willingness to recognise its value even in wider contexts. It is an important signal for Milan and for the future prospects of this field, allowing it to grow whilst maintaining its own identity and interacting increasingly with other worlds.’ 

Looking ahead to next year, designer Francesco Faccin stressed that Italian design has always trodden a fine line between art, research, high craftsmanship, and industry: ‘A humanistic rather than a functionalist approach, that defines “our” way of designing. Sottsass, Mendini, Munari, Mari, Branzi, De Lucchi, Pesce, are just some examples.’ 

As curator Annalisa Rosso stressed, Salone Raritas is a natural evolution within the Salone del Mobile ecosystem. Along with industrial design, which remains central, a number of different, heterogeneous elements are introduced, chosen from all over the world in a conscious response to an ongoing transformation on the international architectural and interior design scene, in which different languages already coexist and support each other.

items.title_es: Salone Raritas: así es como fue
items.content_es:
Los expositores Nina Yashar, Massimo Lunardon, Bruno Botticelli y Francesco Faccin comparten sus pensamientos. Salone Raritas tienden piezas de diseño de edición limitada, antigüedades y alta artesanía a la feria por primera vez este año.

Salone Raritas. Los iconos curados, objetos únicos y piezas de exterior en Pabellón 9 mueven el foco sobre la belleza, la artesanía y la sostenibilidad, entre otras cosas. Curado por Annalisa Rosso, Director Editorial y Asesor Cultural del Salone del Mobile.Milano, y con una exposición diseñada por Formafantasma, la plataforma mostró algunas de las realidades más influyentes de la escena global, así como algunas raras gemas verdaderas. Pedimos a algunos de los expositores que compartan sus opiniones mientras todavía están frescas.

Masimo Lunardon tenía esto que decir: ‘Salone Raritas era una nueva experiencia: refrescante, zumbido, y maravilloso. Visto desde Inside, era la joya en la corona del Salone del Mobile; un pequeño evento que, al mostrar objetos antiguos y piezas de un pasado más reciente, se sentía decididamente innovador y “jóven”. También era muy satisfactorio en términos de entrega, con mucha gente interesante

Bruno Botticelli, presidente de la Associazione Antiquari d’Italia, describió a Salone Raritas como una experiencia interesante sin escasez de propuestas. “No cabe duda de que nos encontramos con un tipo diferente de público, deseoso de encontrar inspiración fresca, pero creo que se necesita un elemento educativo para introducir un mundo desconocido para la mayoría de las personas, especialmente para los no italianos.

Salone Raritas no es, por tanto, un espacio expositivo, sino un difusor de una nueva educación en el diseño.

Nina Yashar, fundadora de Nilufar, también compartió la misma opinión, afirmando que “fue particularmente significativo ver una institución como Salone del Mobile admit gran atención al mundo del diseño coleccionable y, más generalmente, al concepto de rareza. No tanto como una tendencia, sino como una actitud y una receptividad: una manera de observar, seleccionar y conectar objetos y visiones”.

Después de todo, Salone Raritas y Nilufar no son proyectos tan diferentes: "Nilufar se deriva precisamente de este deseo constante de explorar lo que aún no se ha dicho completamente, proporcionando espacio a diferentes idiomas en diálogo entre sí sin jerarquías. En Raritas, encontré esta misma apertura y deseo de crear un espacio dedicado a la investigación, experimentación y visión. "

Por último, mencionó la importancia de los visitantes: “También nos impresionó la calidad y amplitud del público. hubo una oportunidad para interactuar con diseñadores de y profesionales de la industria de diversos orígenes, así como figuras clave en la industria de los muebles. Este amplio interés es, en mi opinión, uno de los factores más significativos para emerger de esta primera edición, destacando una creciente curiosidad hacia el diseño coleccionable, y una disposición mayor para reconocer su valor.

Mirando hacia el próximo año, el diseñador Francesco Faccin destacó que el diseño italiano siempre ha trodido una línea fina entre el arte, la investigación, la alta artesanía y la industria: “Un enfoque humanista más que un enfoque funcionalista, que define “nuestro” modo de diseñar. Sotsass, Mendini, Munari, Mari, Branzi, De Lucchi, Pesce, son sólo algunos ejemplos”.

Como destacó la curadora Annalisa Rosso, Salone Raritas es una evolución natural dentro del ecosistema de Salone del Mobile. Junto con el diseño industrial, que sigue siendo central, se introducen varios elementos heterogéneos diferentes, liberan de todo el mundo en una respuesta consciente a una transformación continua en la escena internacional de diseño editorial e interior, en la que ya coexisten y se apoyan idiomas diferentes.

items.title: Saigon and the Delta: A Taste of Old Saigon
items.content:
In Saigon, the street unfolds according to its own dynamics, serving simultaneously as a corridor, a market, a living room, a playground and a waiting area. In Dino Mehle’s photographs, this interplay is neither organised nor interpreted, but simply documented. The result is a portrait of the city built upon minute coincidences, everyday gestures and compositions destined to last but a few seconds. Street photography has often sought this balance between observation and chance, from William Klein to Martin Parr’s ability to lend the ordinary a slightly unexpected dimension. Mehle operates within the same sphere without seeking dramatic effects. A man smiles whilst sitting on his moped with two dogs perched in front of him; four children turn a pavement into a football pitch; three men are concentrating on a makeshift chessboard. These are scenes in which little happens, yet the essence is captured. The city presents itself above all as a system of relationships. Bodies, signs, electric cables, scooters, plastic chairs and market stalls share the space without any obvious hierarchy.

It is a defining feature of urban life in Ho Chi Minh City, where pavements and roadways continue to function as extensions of domestic and commercial spaces. Mehle captures this density by getting close enough to become part of it, without reducing it to a folkloric element. Colour, too, contributes to the sense of closeness. The deep blue of the chairs and shutters, the red of the signs, the green of the fruit, the almost harsh light of a butcher’s shop: the film captures the imperfections and gives the city a tangible texture. In one of the most direct images, a bare-chested man gives a thumbs-up in front of a row of roast ducks. The portrait arises from the encounter, not from the search for an ideal composition. Subsequently, the rhythm changes. Having left Saigon, the journey continues towards the Mekong Delta and the urban density gradually thins out. It is perhaps in this transition that the work finds its most significant aspect: not in defining a place, but in recording two different paces. On the one hand, a city that seems to constantly anticipate the next frame; on the other, a landscape that invites one to pause. In between, Mehle chooses to proceed with simplicity: walking, waiting and observing whatever comes into the frame.

items.title: What We Saw: Lake Como Design Festival
items.content:
The festival takes on a tangible form when the programme intertwines with the places, objects and people that bring it to life. Over the nine days spent between Como and Lecco, the theme ‘Confine’ found expression above all through tangible elements, such as materials, buildings and the way in which objects occupy spaces. The 2026 edition extended the event to Lecco and local educational institutions for the first time, integrating the event’s geography into the overall project.

Among the most notable aspects was the Contemporary Design Selection, hosted this year in the neoclassical rooms of Villa Saporiti. The contrast between container and content was clearly evident. Pastina’s Soft Monuments transformed the visual weight of monumental sculpture into a padded, tactile volume, whilst Yelyzaveta Rudenok’s Soft Structure Chair softened the rigidity of the wood through kerf cutting.

Elsewhere, the boundary took on a cultural dimension. In her work To Read A Pattern, Marie Vilay integrates Laotian weaving motifs into contemporary production processes, whilst Threads of Origin by Vittorio Di Girolamo and Xenia Kwiatkowska draws on the Amazigh textile traditions of Morocco to explore themes of transmission and belonging. The Long Take by The Happy Few, on the other hand, translates the experience of walking through Shanghai into a carpet, bringing together fragments of the street and urban perceptions. Among the most significant works are Sedia 2 by Mateusz Wappa, a pine structure almost overrun by rough branches of birch, beech and hazel; Constellation by Marijke De Cock, in which beads and ornamental techniques become structures in space; and Porous Boundaries by Barbara Munsel, hand-woven tapestries that visitors do not merely observe but walk through. Olive Tree Console & The Black Chair by Gerard Kuijpers and Schneidersitz by VON DENEN were also based on contrasts: organic material and steel in the former, traditional construction and a minimalist language in the latter.

At Villa del Grumello, Future in the Past approached the same idea from another direction, treating the archive not as something static, but as material that can still be activated through design. Historical references were placed back into circulation: Lupo Borgonovo’s Disegno Nomade enlarged the forms of ancient Eurasian buckles into drawings, etchings and a woven jute rug, while ETEL’s presentation of Lina Bo Bardi brought furniture into dialogue with images of Casa de Vidro and SESC Pompéia. AG Fronzoni’s archive, shown alongside his Collezione 64 for Cappellini, made this relationship even more direct: here, the past was not reconstructed, but allowed to remain useful.

Outside these spaces, the festival demonstrated how objects can transform their surroundings. In the former church of Santa Caterina, the Fine Comune project by Lobby Nomade and Ultrapresent Studio softened the verticality of the religious setting, steering it towards a more horizontal and communal dimension. Acerbis’s Free System and Roberto Sironi’s Hypercode rugs for cc-tapis transformed the nave into a temporary space intended for collective use. In Lecco, Eterno Femminino at the Polytechnic explored the boundary between archetype and stereotype. At Grumello, Nella Natura: storie di chi ha scelto un’altra vita, curated by Paola Manfredi with photographs by Selene Magnolia Gatti, presented six stories of people who have opted for a life between the city and the wilderness.

The most effective projects did not seek to represent the theme of ‘Confine’, but made it tangible: an element to sit on, to cross, to touch or to observe from a different perspective.

items.title: Inside Studio Portaluppi: Architecture, culture and making
items.content:
Some architectural works, once they have gone down in history, may seem untouchable. Studio Portaluppi could well have fallen into this category. After two years behind closed doors, Piero Portaluppi’s historic Milanese studio is reopening in a new form. The premises at 5 Via Morozzo della Rocca return with a different approach to conservation: it is not a question of freezing the past, but rather of allowing it to generate new possibilities. The historic studio, designed by Piero Portaluppi and completed in 1939, has become the new headquarters of Filippo Taidelli Architecture and, at the same time, of Studio Portaluppi, a transdisciplinary laboratory curated by Julia Koropoulos.

Taidelli, Portaluppi’s great-grandson, has intervened whilst avoiding both a philological reconstruction and a contemporary gesture aimed at creating contrast. The result appears more nuanced. In the images, the old and the new seem almost to overlap: the walnut panelling meets metal structures, white surfaces and a new grid of light; the openings are transformed into frames; the greenery of the garden visually extends into the interiors. It is a form of architecture composed of subtle shifts, in which distinguishing what dates from 1939 from what belongs to 2026 is not always straightforward. And this is probably the central aspect.

In the meeting room, the polychrome marble floor comprises over five hundred pieces sourced from quarries across the globe, some of which are now impossible to find. Portaluppi had also conceived this surface as a sample display for clients. At its centre stands the walnut table, reconstructed according to the original drawings. Viewed from above, the floor evokes the forms of a modernist collage, where the finish becomes an atlas of colours, origins and periods.

In other parts of the project, more playful elements emerge. Portholes, passageways, openings and hidden mechanisms echo the ironic and almost mechanical quality already present in Portaluppi’s imagination. Even the air-raid shelter, once forgotten beneath the garden and rediscovered thanks to historical drawings, has been reintegrated into the life of the studio and made accessible via a metal drawbridge integrated into the flooring.

The reopening of the space stands out for its value beyond mere restoration. Following two years of renovation, the former private office of Piero Portaluppi now houses Filippo Taidelli Architecture, while the entrance hall, meeting room, courtyard and rediscovered underground bunker form Studio Portaluppi, opening the building to a new public and cultural life. Its programme will begin in autumn 2026 under the title C’est l’heure de bien faire — “It’s time to do things well” — with exhibitions, workshops, talks, concerts and site-specific interventions bringing architecture into dialogue with materials, craftsmanship and research. Rather than becoming a monument dedicated to its architect, the studio returns as an active cultural infrastructure. Memory, after all, can also be preserved through continued use. Perhaps the most contemporary way of inhabiting Portaluppi’s space is precisely to avoid treating it as a relic.

items.title: Daimonos: Where the Divine Leaves a Trace
items.content:
In the Daimonos series, the sacred does not manifest itself explicitly. It is enough for it to leave a trace. An empty room bathed in an almost unreal light, a moth suspended against the sky, an out-of-focus cross: in Dimitris Fodiadis’s photographs, the human presence seems to recede gradually, whilst what remains takes on the weight of an apparition.

The title refers to the daimon of ancient Greek culture, an entity intermediate between humans and gods, neither strictly divine nor earthly. It is precisely this ambiguous condition that defines the visual vocabulary of the series. There is no clear distinction between the spiritual and the material: a landscape can be transformed into a place of worship, an animal can take on the power of a symbol, and an everyday object can become a relic.

The image of the sheep, motionless on the mountainside, seems to belong both to a pastoral landscape and to Christian iconography. Shortly afterwards, a bunch of grapes appears on the chest of a human silhouette. This reference can be interpreted through the lens of wine and the Eucharistic tradition, but also through the figure of Dionysus, the god of intoxication, metamorphosis and the blurring of individual boundaries. Paganism and Christianity are not set in opposition: they overlap, suggesting how the images through which we represent the transcendent continue to influence one another.

Even the body, when it appears, is never actually shown. It is a silhouette, a surface onto which to project meanings. Elsewhere, it disappears entirely. What remains is a lit chandelier in a bare room, a piece of fabric abandoned on the floor, a cross reduced to a patch of light. There is something of the Surrealist logic in this transformation of the ordinary through seemingly simple juxtapositions: not so much a desire to construct a fantasy world, as a desire to render the familiar alien.

The blue that dominates Daimonos helps to keep every image in a state of ambiguity, as if it had been photographed in the moment just before daybreak or just after nightfall. Even the landscape loses its definition: low-hanging clouds obscure the horizon, whilst an iridescent shape crosses the sky like an optical illusion or a vision.

It is here that the series finds its most intriguing tension. It does not seek to photograph the divine, but rather what happens when one begins to seek it. And suddenly anything — an animal, a shadow, an empty room — can appear as a sign.

items.title: Drifting: A Place to Pass Through
items.content: In Drifting, Tokyo takes center stage, not just as a setting but as a character in its own right. Rikuto Uchiumi captures the city in its everyday moments: think glistening wet streets, plain residential buildings, exposed pipes, tiled walls, and lush greenery burdened by rain. These spaces are meant for simply passing through, yet here they form the backdrop for a fashion narrative where the theme of not quite fitting in prevails. Haruno navigates these scenes like a delightful disruption. Stylist Maiko Karima cleverly juxtaposes the neighborhood’s practicality with high fashion—imagine a flowing white dress paired with oversized round sunglasses nestled amid ordinary homes, or a ghostly figure in a frayed white knit and an exaggerated wig strolling under an umbrella. In other shots, a striking all-black outfit with a crisp white collar and sharp heels transforms the underside of an apartment building into something akin to a stage. There’s a nod to Japanese New Wave cinema in the way Uchiumi highlights these overlooked spaces, reminiscent of the quiet detachment found in the works of Hiroshi Sugimoto or the urban solitude captured by Wim Wenders. Yet, Uchiumi steers clear of glamorizing the city. His Tokyo feels authentically lived-in—with a toilet door, an air-conditioning unit, a plant on a speaker, and clothes piled in a room all given equal importance to the clothing on display. This balance is what makes Drifting resonate. Fashion often demands its surroundings to embrace fantasy, but here, it feels as though fantasy has intruded on a space it doesn’t completely fit. Haruno oscillates between different worlds: inside and out, styled and disguised, visible yet somehow removed from her environment. Even the rain plays its part without theatrics. It leaves everything with a subtle sheen, allowing the slower pace of the city to reveal its often-overlooked details. Drifting crafts its unique atmosphere right there, in that delicate space between truly living in a place and merely passing through it.

items.title: Video of the Week: DEAR [NAME] directed by Amara Abbas
items.content:
DEAR [NAME], the four-minute short film, takes the familiar language of corporate rejection and turns it into a spoken-word performance about what remains after the inbox has moved on: self-doubt, frustration, resilience and the growing suspicion that nobody was looking in the first place. The script is built from real rejection lines sent to ethnic minority candidates, giving an anonymous and automated language back to the people receiving it.

Starring Ebenezer Gyau and produced by new—land, the film sits at the centre of Reject the Rejections, a campaign by People Like Us, created in partnership with independent creative agency Worth Your While. It responds to the increasing role of automated systems in recruitment and, more specifically, to the lack of transparency around how they make decisions.

The film makes this largely invisible process physical. Its entire world is contained inside an anonymous, windowless waiting room. The setting has the logic of an office but none of its purpose. People wait to be assessed without knowing who, or what, is assessing them.

That uncertainty shapes the film’s visual and sonic language. Corporate phrases are repeated until their politeness begins to feel mechanical; stamps, footsteps and falling paper become part of the rhythm beneath the monologue. The mirror turns observation back onto the person being observed. By the final reveal, one rejected candidate becomes part of a larger room of people waiting for the same answer. What begins as an individual experience gradually exposes a system designed to operate at scale.

DEAR [NAME] is less interested in explaining automation than in showing what it feels like to encounter it from the other side. The following conversation with the film’s director and co-writer, Amara Abbas, looks behind its construction — from the waiting room and two-way glass to the use of sound, 35mm film and the decision to turn the language of rejection into something that can finally answer back.

 

Gaia V. Marraffa: From the modular chairs to the wall-mounted phone, the waiting room has the unsettling quality of a Kafkaesque non-place. How did you use the physical space to heighten that sense of alienation?

Amara Abbas: Very Kafka. A waiting room is already a kind of transient non-space, so setting the film there gave us a strong foundation to build from. With the set design we stripped away anything that could root you in a specific place or time. The wall-mounted phone we recognize as a mode of communication but in the film we don’t see any dialogue or conversation so for me it almost feels one-way, like the mirror. The doorway looks like it leads to another hallway and gives this illusion its one room in a larger maze-like space. The room itself doesn’t have a ton of personality or context and I think it creates the sort of disorienting feeling that could drive you crazy, especially because there are no windows. You would probably start to wonder how long you’ve been there. I think the mirror also does a lot of work to create the feeling of being watched. And you are physically with others but alone. So combined all these elements created a sense of psychological isolation.

GVM: The “REJECTED” stamp, the footsteps, the sound of paper hitting the floor — the rhythms of office life gradually become part of the film’s musical language. What led you to turn these everyday sounds into the beat beneath the monologue?

AA: I think sound is such a special tool for film, sometimes more effective than image. I love the idea of sound design and music existing as one organism, where you don’t necessarily realize when one ends and the other begins. Here it felt like they needed to be of the same code/speak the same language.

The most important element in this film is actually the words. They are the soul of the film and carry the piece. So I felt the sounds needed to punctuate and support that. Underneath the monologue, the everyday monotonous sounds became a way to add brutality. The stamp sound specifically is like a kind of drum or pulse, something that was brutal and unmistakable. All of these everyday sounds building to me are like the feeling of death by a thousand paper cuts. I think that’s the feeling of constant rejection too, it’s not usually one dramatic blow, but something that accumulates and wears you down in a way. On some instinctual level those sounds become a vessel for that feeling.

GVM: The one-way glass introduces ideas of invisibility, surveillance and a divided sense of self. What does the mirror — and the act of seeing without being seen — represent for you within the film?

AA: There’s a line that captures this feeling better than I can express it, where S.E. Hinton wrote, “…they make me think of a two-way mirror. Like you could feel somebody on the other side watching you, but the only reflections you saw were your own.” That really resonated with me – it’s something that operates more subconsciously. In the film when our main character looks through the glass, all he sees is his own reflection. So in a way I think he sees himself as the problem. Constant rejection does that, it has this way of turning inward, you start questioning if it’s you, if you’re not enough, if you should just work harder. There’s an internalization that happens and it can feel very personal, even though it’s structural by design. In that way, I think it creates a false sense of self and a false sense of truth where what you’re seeing isn’t necessarily reality.

With the element of surveillance the mirror introduces, I wanted it to express a panopticon-like quality that exists within modern office culture and in the hiring process, like being watched by an unknown authority. It’s not so dissimilar to prisons or interrogation rooms, that sort of power imbalance. But here I’m more interested in the human and psychological aspect of the character and how these structures might affect someone over time. What’s the aftermath of what these systems do to someone, what’s their interior and how do they process and deal with that?

GVM: There is a striking moment when the crowd of candidates waiting in the shadows is finally revealed, exposing a version of diversity that exists more as corporate image than genuine inclusion. How did you approach translating that contradiction into the film’s visual language?

AA: It’s funny, I think it actually just happened quite organically. With the very last shot we originally just wanted to make sure we had an image of everyone waiting. Bored or tired, like they’d been there a while, but the positions of each of them, their looks and expressions had an iconography to it that reminded of something like The Breakfast Club. Somehow rebellious in spirit. On the surface because they are all people of color I think it reads like diversity as aesthetic, or kind of like something you’d see on a hiring page. But spending time and sitting in that moment after the characters journey, after we’ve visibly seen these people reduced to a box and to never be chosen creates another emotion. You feel and take in each individual life and hopefully it lets you get past the superficial and to something deeper. I think the moment of him walking back to his seat to the final shot gives us space and time to take in each person in the room and remind us he is just one of many.

GVM: Your work moves between large-scale productions and films with a more explicitly social and political urgency. Where does DEAR [NAME] sit within the evolution of your practice and your visual language as a filmmaker?

AA: I think those choices come more from feeling and instinct or whatever is speaking to me. They are all different facets of what I’m interested in and resonate with. The subject matter I work on often does affect people from my world in one way or another, which is likely why I’m drawn to it and what I want to see more of on screen. I guess you could say my existence is social/political because of my name and where I’m from so even when a project isn’t explicitly about that, the perspective comes with me just from how I experience the world. DEAR [NAME] is very special in terms of personal connection to the material and its disruptive honesty. Everyone who worked on the film also felt that same connection and understood the material demanded to be handled with great care and urgency, as it should be told.

With my visual language, I want to keep challenging myself and keep evolving as an artist. These days, the more I learn about photography and cinema, the more precise and simple I actually want to be. I think restraint often lets emotions come through more clearly. You’re able to just observe and absorb more, it’s like a meditation. I really love that. Shooting on 35mm for this project specifically, I wanted to bring precision into the worldbuilding, the choice of compositions, and just stay close to the character, letting his true emotions lead everything. Overall it gave the film a more formal quality which I’ve been really interested to explore more of, and I’m excited to see where it takes me next.

GVM: You’ve described DEAR [NAME] as a film interested in saying the quiet part out loud. At a time when social divisions feel increasingly visible, what role do you think cinema can play in confronting them and perhaps in breaking some of those barriers down?

AA: With this film specifically the nature of the monologue actually is saying the quiet part out loud. It’s pretty unapologetic and direct. With the kind of change that People Like Us are trying to create, it felt very necessary to be a bit more radical in some way and use the spoken word format to begin al dialogue, where you fully experience what is in this character’s heart and mind so brazenly.

I think cinema itself is its own language, one that is universal. Anyone from anywhere can feel something from it. That’s its gift. It also allows us to spend time with someone. And if you spend enough time with someone, you can relate to them, understand them, even fall in love with them, in a way you might not typically be able to in reality. It’s quite intimate, giving you access to cultures and people from a world entirely different from your own. To me that intimacy is what makes cinema so special. The world does feel increasingly polarizing, many people are quite firm in their beliefs before encountering another perspective, and I mean this on everything – from the smallest things to the big, important things. But if a film can get someone to sit with a person, for 5 minutes or for 90, I wonder if it can disarm some of that defensiveness and invite more curiosity and connection. It opens up another truth or way of seeing, and hopefully from there inspires conversation.

items.title: Us, Collectors
items.content:
When you meet someone, do you ever try to imagine what unsuspecting things they might be obsessed with? Or, when spotting something unusual or kooky, do you ever try to imagine what kind of person would do anything to get their hands on it?

Tell me what you collect, and I will tell you who you are—it’s a fun game to play, especially when you wave off the realm of the plausible and go wild, which is exactly how it works in real life.

In fact, sometimes the correct answers are so seemingly random that it feels like anything could belong to anyone, so is there even an

y point in trying to make a reasonable guess?

But somehow, from the least original to the most blindsiding, every combination of collector and collection ultimately makes sense.

 

This is because one is the reflection of the other, and the nature of this reflection is either specular, or revelatory—that is, it either duplicates things as they already appear, or it magnifies something otherwise invisible.

For example, it makes sense that a young and quirky chef might reserve a whole kitchen shelf to her varied assortment of little vintage eggcups, and be thrilled to tell you everything about them—after all, it is in perfect harmony with the person we know her to be. 

It strikes us as funny and yet completely plausible that a stern banker might spend his office hours itching to go home, take his expensive suit off, and finish painting his horde of miniature cyborgs. 

But how? How can it make sense? And yet it does.

For many of us, there are parts of who we are that exist jealously tucked away in pockets of our life; in apparent contradiction with the rest of it, and thus kept separate. The figurine, the card, the bauble, are keepsakes from a private dimension that we don’t witness, but that we can intuit by absence: the missing dot by which all the others connect. 

 

Hidden or not, this side of us can be detected, even if just in retrospect.

It’s as if the nature of the collection, or perhaps even the very fact of having one, inevitably seeps through the persona we embody in front of the world and peeks out from its folds, vivid or faint, but either way surely there.

And in turn, in a sort of alchemical reciprocity, that hidden part of us also peeks out from our collection, as if infused into its surface by countless gestures of devotion—assembling, polishing, cataloguing, but also playing, caressing, turning over and inside out, feeling weig

ht and texture in the hands.

These objects are physical tokens of the things that move us, lending tactility to the abstraction of emotions, passions, ideals, and dispositions that compose the mosaic that is “us.”

It is easy, then, to understand the urge not only to own, but to amass and duly honor these sort of simulacra, of effigies of the self—and how indulging in this urge can sometimes surmount both reason and measure, and any attempt at concealment.

With each touch, the collection inevitably rubs off on the collector, and vice versa.

 

So, let’s play.

Take a look at these pictures: who are these people? What drives them to collect those specific things? Is it childhood nostalgia, a hobby turned mission, wishful self-projection, or maybe a very elaborate inner joke?

There are no truths here—these stories are entirely yours to tell.

items.title: A Matter of Taste: what remains after eating
items.content:
Eating is one of the most common acts of daily life. However, when viewed in the context of its surroundings, it takes on broader meanings: work, privilege, survival, memory or a sense of belonging. It is against this backdrop that the fifth edition of the Yeast Photo Festival, entitled A Matter of Taste, takes place in Galatina from 11 September to 8 November. The event focuses not so much on the image of food itself as on the systems that make its existence possible. The selected photographs avoid the refinement typical of contemporary food photography and instead show peppers pierced on skewers, broad beans scattered on a blanket, freshly caught fish, handwritten recipes or a frying pan on the hob. Food is restored to its material nature, as something to be gathered, prepared, preserved and passed down. In an age when photographing meals has become a habitual gesture, the exhibition offers a different approach. Whilst digital images tend to transform food into an object of desire, here it becomes a means of observing what usually remains outside the frame.

In the project ‘Daughters of the Sea’, Forough Alaei documents the fisherwomen of the Iranian island of Hengam, where their work is shaped by legal and social constraints, in a context that is at risk of disappearing. In ‘The Last Generation’, Bob Miller portrays American farming families at a time of transition, when the passing of land from one generation to the next can no longer be taken for granted. The theme of transmission emerges in several works. In Pier Costantini’s photographic diary, his father Guerino’s recipes form a domestic archive. In Marco Zorzanello’s ‘La Panarda’, an Abruzzese feast of over fifty courses becomes a communal occasion in which no one is excluded. Even the simplest images suggest that a culture is preserved through repeated gestures. A Matter of Taste addresses the theme of food without presenting it as an object of desire. In this context, ‘taste’ concerns who is able to take part in the meal, who prepares it, and what stories make their way onto the plate – as well as what might be lost.

items.title: A Scene by Nicolas Sayed
items.content:
In the temperate darkness that envelops the city’s outskirts, time seems to stand still and fashion transcends the catwalk to take the form of physical expression, attitude and identity. In the visual project “A Scene by Nicolas Sayed”, director and director of photography Nicolas Darwiche, sketches out a fringe space where urban subculture intertwines with a cinematic narrative. This is neither a trailer nor a conventional short film, but rather a visual fragment taken from an imaginary film, which manifests itself in the perception of both the creator and the viewer. The protagonists, Huy Thanh and Melvin Niamkey, portrayed against a metal fence overlooking the railway tracks, embody a nonchalance typical of contemporary menswear, influenced by skate culture and street style. The oversized, relaxed-fit garments, the platinum-blonde hair shaped by the dim light, the thin chains and the glasses with understated frames all help to define the characters’ social background and sense of belonging.

This work forms part of a strand of fashion photography that favours a poetic and marginal realism over artificial aesthetic solutions. The everyday gesture of asking for a lighter, the exchange of observations on memories of Paris and the sharing of a cigarette lend a chance encounter the significance of a generational manifesto. It is a dialogue between seemingly distant spheres, set to a subdued soundtrack and an analogue visual texture. In a visual context often characterised by superficial approaches, ‘A Scene by Nicolas Sayed’ illustrates how the language of fashion, when confronted with arthouse cinema, can convey the discontinuities, irony and authenticity of human relationships. This experiment, discreet and nostalgic in nature, sparks interest in a possible narrative extension.

items.title: Video of the Week: PAMELA directed by Albert Font
items.content:
In PAMELA, Albert Font explores the theme of beauty through subtraction. Shot on 16mm film, his latest visual project moves away from the speed and excess of the digital imagination, offering instead an intimate space in which rebirth is intertwined with a renewed sense of self.

At the heart of the film is the model Natalie Tischler, whose presence defines the rhythm of the images: slow movements, minimalist gestures, hands resting on her neck and back. The body does not seek an external gaze, but seems to recognise itself. Intimacy is built through small details, in which even the clothes contribute to the scene without overwhelming it. Fashion blends with the figure, accompanying its movements and transformation.

Font focuses on the relationship between light, surface and material. The grain of the 16mm film emerges from the shadows, lending the images an almost tangible warmth, whilst the cold, desaturated background keeps the setting in a more detached dimension. Two distinct elements are woven into this composition: a greyhound, motionless and statuesque, evoking a classical and controlled elegance, and a red rose submerged in water, the sole bold chromatic accent and a symbol of restrained fragility.

Roman Lombardi’s composition for strings follows the same logic. PAMELA does not construct a dramatic narrative, but proceeds through images, gestures and atmospheres. The result is a portrait of the female form that avoids exaggeration and draws its strength from restraint. For Font, becoming is not a spectacular transformation, but something more subtle: a different way of inhabiting one’s own body, and of looking at it.

items.title: Walter Pfeiffer: ‘I Don’t Believe In Nostalgia’
items.content:
If you don’t know Walter Pfeiffer by name, you will almost certainly recognise his images. Something about their high-contrast, terribly colourful, tightly framed lexicon probably feels utterly familiar… 

If you agree, but cannot quite put your finger on the reason why, a clue lies in an essay by the co-curator of Pfeiffer’s latest retrospective titled In Good Company, published in the accompanying photobook by the same name. In it, Nicola Trezzi describes Pfeiffer as a ‘prophet of image-making,’ and outlines how the artist anticipated many of the visual codes that define social media-era fashion imagery today.

Pfeiffer, then, feels remarkably familiar because we constantly encounter images like his on our Instagram feeds, where—for better or worse—culture has become increasingly cyclical and self-referential. A good part of contemporary photography seems to exist in a suspended state, somewhere outside of “the contemporary,” if such a term still retains any meaning. The persistent relevance of Pfeiffer’s work raises an obvious question: why do these images continue to be synonymous with our ultra-digital present, when they were made by an artist now in his eighties?

Perhaps the answer lies in a paradox. While Pfeiffer’s photographic language has been so readily adopted in the digital sphere, its origins are resolutely grounded in the physical. ‘I like paradoxes,’ Pfeiffer wrote by email, ‘they make life more exciting!’

The artist began by photographing friends, and friends of friends who dropped by his apartment in Zurich during the 1970s and 1980s. ‘I treated the people I photographed as if they were stars,’ Pfeiffer tells me over email, ‘They were beautiful and they appeared even more beautiful in my pictures. I felt I must chase and capture beauty.’  

The emphasis on connection follows Pfeiffer throughout his career and forms a central pillar of both his recent retrospective and publication. The title of each, In Good Company, speaks to the artist’s collaborative process, his reliance on friends as subjects, and the cherished objects and things that populate his world. Personal connection and tactile reality emanates from these images. At times, one feels almost able to hear a loud billowing laugh while looking at them; they are that evocative.

By the time the digital turn came to be, however, Pfeiffer was already in his sixties. After years of toiling in relative obscurity—certainly as far as outside of Europe is concerned—he received some of his earliest fashion editorial commissions from Dutch magazine publishers Gert Jonkers and Jop van Bennekom in the early 2000s, who would later launch Fantastic Man in 2005 and The Gentlewoman in 2010 and continue to commission Pfeiffer.

From there, the number of commissions only continued to grow, along with the prestige of the publications seeking his work; French Vogue, Dazed, Self Service, and i-D all embraced Pfeiffer’s irresistible blend of humour, vibrancy, and seduction, recognising that his work had something utterly contemporary about it, despite the fact that it wasn’t quite as contemporary as one might think. It’s a visual style the artist had developed—and stayed true to—for the preceding thirty-odd years.

Meanwhile, other photographers and countless publications appear to reference Pfeiffer continuously online. This points towards another—and perhaps more intriguing—reason for his enduring influence. Not only do his images evoke the tactile realities for which we may long, they also fit neatly within the algorithmic framework of the attention economy.

To borrow photo editor Emily Keegin’s viral breakdown of the subject on the podcast The Cutting Room Floor, fashion photography today largely favours cropped subjects captured in frames that are ‘just about clothes and space.’ These visually clean and quickly captivating images perform better on feeds. They do not require prolonged attention, like a detailed landscape photograph or narrative scene might. Effective simplicity reigns. It certainly does in Pfeiffer’s images, which rarely feature more than two people, and which hardly ever are zoomed out enough for spectators to see both a subject’s face and the lower half of their body simultaneously.

The digital life of Pfeiffer’s connective images also play into our collective sense that our world seems to have lost something. The nostalgic or “backwards-looking” language of contemporary photography in the post-digital era is well documented; as today, hoards of historians of photography attempt to grapple with the reasons why photographers and spectators alike continue to turn to previous forms of the medium, and to value the analogue over the digital. Of nostalgia, Pfeiffer writes, ‘I do not believe in nostalgia, and even today, with all that is happening, I want to keep in contact with the real world. I love to connect. Technology is just a tool, we use it the way we want.’

Perhaps, however, it is precisely because many very powerful people are not using new technology in a way some of us want, that we look to nostalgic forms of image making for clues as to how to access previous ways of living, relating and existing. In this way, nostalgia in our culture is rather positive, as the past can be viewed as an opening. 

Trezzi believes a slippery relationship with time and the contemporary is another prophetic aspect of the artist’s work; ‘he made sure that dates would never rule over the image, leaving us to wonder whether an image was taken in the 1970s or the 2000s. In a time of suspended temporality (in the same way the term contemporary art has been dragged around for decades now), this becomes a seminal condition,’ writes Trezzi. Pfeiffer’s retrospective also unfolds thematically, as opposed to chronologically. Pfeiffer clarified to me over email that ‘[Nicolas] writes that although I know all the dates, he believes I do not write them because I wanted to keep things open to let people wonder and imagine.’

No matter the reason, commissioning fashion houses and magazines don’t seem to care. The artist is perhaps more solicited than ever before. ‘As I get older, I feel I have less time,’ Pfeiffer tells me. ‘Therefore I work all the time. I want to achieve as much as possible, considering that time is limited, especially for me.’

items.title: A preview of what’s to come: Lake Como Design Festival
items.content:
A piece of furniture might be examined starting with its form or the designer’s name, or, vice versa, beginning with an engraving, a sample of wood, an archive photograph or a drawing that has been preserved for years. It is this latter approach that characterises the Lake Como Design Festival.

From 12 to 20 September, the Festival returns for its eighth edition with ‘Confine’, a title broad enough to cover geographies, materials, disciplines and generations. This year, the festival is also physically expanding its territory, moving for the first time between Como and Lecco, whilst villas, archives, schools, studios and spaces not usually part of the exhibition circuit become part of the programme. It is a format deliberately distinct from the concentrated nature of a trade fair. Design is encountered whilst walking through the city and, above all, by observing it in the very place where it has been situated.

Research remains at the heart of this edition. At Villa del Grumello, ‘Future in the Past’ brings together archives, collections and contemporary interventions around a rather simple question: what happens when the past is utilised rather than merely preserved? Figures such as AG Fronzoni and Lina Bo Bardi feature here; Etel is exhibiting some of the furniture she designed in Brazil. These are not nostalgic references. Rather, they serve to remind us how issues now considered contemporary have long been part of design practice.

The archive makes a return at various points throughout the festival, including at Ico Parisi’s space, which is hosting an exhibition dedicated to his collaboration with Giuliano Collina. Yet what emerges from the whole is not so much an obsession with the past as with the process itself: drawings, sketches, techniques and relationships become tools for understanding how a project takes shape. It is an approach that well reflects the identity the festival has built up in recent years, one that is closer to research and material culture than to the logic of a major commercial event.

Providing a counterpoint is the Contemporary Design Selection, hosted for the first time in the neoclassical Villa Saporiti. Curated by Giovanna Massoni and directed by Francesca Prandelli, it brings together over fifty participants from around thirty countries. Ceramics, glass, wood, metal, textiles, biomaterials and waste materials paint a picture in which it is difficult to identify a single aesthetic — fortunately. What is more evident, however, is the interest in the way things are produced: who makes them, where the materials come from, what knowledge is preserved and what can be changed.

Then design transcends the object itself. At the Conservatoire, it becomes sound with Atto Puro; at the Politecnico di Lecco, it intersects with research into the Alpine landscape and its instability. With Oltre al Vedere, even Vico Magistretti’s famous Eclisse is stripped of its visual form: a sensory version allows it to be understood through touch and sound, prompting us to question what it truly means to know an object beyond sight.

It is perhaps here that ‘Confine’ becomes less of a theme and more of a stance. Somewhere between an archive and a new prototype, between craftsmanship and technology, between an eighteenth-century villa and a contemporary experiment, the festival does not so much seek to establish where one discipline ends and another begins. It seems more interested in what happens in between.

And for nine days, by the lake, design has plenty of opportunity to do that.

items.title: Por Mi Tango: A Language Of Desire
items.content:
In tango, even before the steps, there is an unspoken agreement: two bodies establish how much space to allow one another. Drawing closer means, at the same time, exposing oneself and offering resistance, trusting the other without ever looking away. “Por Mi Tango” draws on this tension, born from a concept deeply tied to Giuditta Vettese’s passion for tango and brought to life through her art direction alongside the team. The visual project strips the dance of its most recognisable imagery to focus on what remains when the music seems to have faded away. In Alessandro Merlo’s images, red does not merely accompany the scene: it envelops it entirely. Upholstered walls, curtains, clothes and skin merge into a single chromatic substance, transforming the space into a sort of inner chamber. The parallel with the use of colour in Pedro Almodóvar’s films is immediate, where red can simultaneously embody desire, danger and theatricality.

Here, however, the saturation takes on an almost claustrophobic quality: there is no real escape from the scene, only bodies that emerge and fade into the shadows. The tango is thus broken down into its constituent parts. One leg crosses over the other, a hand rests on a hip, two figures draw closer until they become almost mirror images of one another. In one of the shots, a face painted white abruptly interrupts the sensuality of the sequence, introducing a disturbing element, reminiscent of a mask and the theatrical realm. In another, a solitary body assumes the posture of the dance without a partner: the gesture survives the encounter. It is perhaps here that “Por Mi Tango” reveals its most evocative image. Desire is not depicted as a linear path towards the other, but rather as a circular motion that constantly returns to the one who feels it.

The two dancers may be lovers, adversaries, or reflections of the same figure. When they finally embrace, the embrace does not resolve this ambiguity: it amplifies it. ROT’s costumes also form part of the choreography. Cuts, back openings, form-fitting fabrics and vertical pleats follow the body without making it entirely accessible to the gaze. Fashion thus becomes an integral part of the movement, a surface that both reveals and conceals. Rather than narrating the tango, “Por Mi Tango” captures its essence: that minimal, unstable distance that separates desiring someone from desiring to be desired.

items.title: Lost in Tokyo: Woven into the City
items.content:
For decades, Tokyo has been portrayed as the quintessential symbol of modern-day speed. Yet what happens when the world’s fastest-paced metropolis becomes a setting for waiting? ‘Lost in Tokyo’ turns this perspective on its head, replacing movement with stillness and transforming the urban space into an emotional landscape. In this vision, the city is not a spectacular backdrop, but a discreet presence that invites us to notice what usually escapes our attention: moments of pause, detours, those instants when the body slows down whilst the urban fabric carries on with its course. Shot predominantly on film and using only natural light, Elie Bianco’s photo series creates an atmosphere that belongs more to memory than to the present. The grain of the images softens the frenetic pace and presents a Tokyo far removed from the hyper-technological aesthetic often associated with its Western image.

The reference is not to the neon lights of “Blade Runner”, but rather to the suspended melancholy of Sofia Coppola’s “Lost in Translation” or the contemplative pace of Wim Wenders’ “Perfect Days”, where everyday life takes on an almost ritualistic quality. In this context, fashion engages in a dialogue with architecture rather than overshadowing it. Openwork knits, crochet, floral embroidery and open weaves create a language defined as much by absences as by presences. It is a slow, artisanal craft that seems to contrast with the geometric rigidity of concrete, tiles and infrastructure. However, the contrast does not create tension: the garments ultimately absorb the city, reflecting its hidden rhythm. The floral motifs echo the street lamps dotting the alleyways, the open weaves harmonise with the electric cables criss-crossing the sky, and the form-fitting silhouettes express a vulnerability that the environment amplifies.

The protagonist, Enya, does not wander through Tokyo like a modern flâneuse, but experiences it with an almost alienating calm. Standing at the corner of a traditional, lantern-lit street, motionless in the middle of the road or suspended on a footbridge, she seems to defy the logic of having a destination. Her gaze is not searching for anything: she observes, waits, and allows the landscape to wash over her. Consequently, the city ceases to be a mere backdrop and becomes a measure of inner distance. It is precisely this choice that makes ‘Lost in Tokyo’ more profound than a simple tale of ‘lost’ youth. Being lost is not a dramatic condition, but an act of silent resistance. In an age that measures time in terms of productivity and speed, allowing oneself a pause becomes a meaningful gesture. Elie Bianco’s images suggest that, perhaps, the only way to rediscover a place is to stop, at least for a moment, looking for it.

items.title: UNIVERSE CONTAINED
items.content:
Space is often mistaken for emptiness. As if silence were the absence of life, rather than evidence of everything it has absorbed. But space remembers. It stretches around memory, desire, grief, instinct. It holds traces of movement long after bodies disappear from it. 

A woman moves through space differently. She does not simply occupy it; she alters its emotional temperature. Presence becomes something expansive, difficult to contain within fixed borders. She carries softness beside severity, restraint beside hunger, solitude beside sensuality. Never singular, never fixed, she exists as an accumulation: of past selves, imagined selves, inherited selves, hidden selves. Entire interior worlds coexisting at once. 

In emptiness, these layers become visible. Without distraction, space begins to echo the architecture of the self. Corners feel like memory. Light becomes almost tactile. Silence sharpens perception. What first appears vacant slowly reveals itself to be dense with emotional residue. 

There is a particular power in flourishing without excess. In discovering that abundance is not always material, but internal. That beauty can emerge not from decoration or fullness, but from tension, atmosphere, and the ability to remain expansive even within limitation. 

Perhaps this is why emptiness can feel strangely transformative. It leaves room for contradiction to surface. For fragility and confidence to exist together. For stillness to reveal movement underneath it. A woman becomes not one identity, but many unfolding simultaneously—shifting between presence and absence, exposure and protection, intimacy and distance.

items.title: An Inhabitant Among What Remains, Cicadas Beyond the Engawa
items.content:
Houses are never static. They absorb gestures, preserve memories, and change alongside those who pass through them. In Inhabitant, Steph Hayashi’s editorial transforms a traditional Japanese dwelling into a living, breathing organism, where architecture, memory and fashion influence one another. It is not simply an interior that houses a body, but a space that seems to have already recorded its presence, as if every room held the memory of those who lived there before. The images weave a narrative built around doorways. The engawa – the transitional space between interior and exterior typical of Japanese architecture – becomes the symbolic heart of the entire project: a boundary that does not separate, but connects. It is there that Nodoka Usami’s body appears suspended, seated on the edge of the house, whilst natural light filters through the undulating glass and blurs the contours.

The figure seems to belong as much to the landscape as to the building, as if it were an extension of the material that surrounds it. Steph Hayashi, the photographer, avoids any folkloric imagery associated with Japan. Rather, she evokes that aesthetic sensibility which Jun’ichirō Tanizaki described in “In Praise of Shadows”: a world in which beauty arises from half-light, from wear and tear, from surfaces that time has slowly transformed. The weathered walls, the worn wood and the floors reflecting a soft light are not merely scenographic elements, they contribute to the construction of the visual identity just as much as the garments themselves. Fashion, consequently, relinquishes the idea of being the absolute protagonist. The garments oscillate between materiality and lightness: knitted fabrics, fluid silks, lace and structured volumes interact with the house without ever dominating it.

In one of the shots, an olive-green fabric drapes along the geometry of the veranda, whilst in another the lilac satin cuts across the corridor like a foreign presence, introducing a chromatic tension that disrupts the tranquillity of the interiors. Further on, the reimagined kimono and the printed dress seem instead to absorb the hues of the wood, almost as if they had been dyed by the space itself. The photography, too, follows this logic of coexistence. The shots alternate between strictly architectural compositions and close-up portraits in which the model’s gaze breaks the silence with an almost restless intensity. The house observes just as much as it is observed. Inhabitant thus suggests a broader reflection on contemporary living. Hayashi imagines the home as an emotional archive, capable of shaping those who live there just as much as it is shaped by their presence. Clothing, then, is not just something one wears, but another layer of this ongoing relationship between body, memory and place.

items.title: Harlem Labs: Survival and Ambition
items.content:
Harlem has always been more than a neighborhood; it is a living, breathing inheritance. From the electrifying heights of the Harlem Renaissance to the contemporary street corners that dictate global fashion and art, it remains a sanctuary where culture is forged, tested, and passed down. Drawing inspiration from the iconic narrative of The Wiz, a new visual project from Harlem Labs honors that deep legacy while charting an entirely original path forward for the modern creative.

At its heart, the project is a striking visual story about return, transformation, and the quiet courage required to be truly seen. Set against the vibrant, layered backdrop of Harlem, it follows a new generation of visionaries navigating the complex intersections of identity, survival, ambition, and community. Much like Dorothy’s journey down the yellow brick road, these artists eventually confront a universal truth: everything they have been searching for has existed within themselves, and within the community standing right beside them, all along.

The project is spearheaded by Harlem Labs, a multidisciplinary creative studio founded by Jamont Hanshaw that focuses on visual storytelling, creative direction, and collaborative artistry. For Hanshaw and the studio, this effort reflects the chaotic, beautiful reality of “creating while becoming.” It emphasizes the desperate need for spaces where emerging and historically underrepresented artists do not just survive, but feel profoundly supported, visible, and free to experiment without restraint.

Far transcending a standard fashion story, the work serves as a cultural manifesto. It poses a fundamental question: what happens when artists stop waiting for institutional permission and simply start building worlds of their own?

By rootedness in ancestral pride and an unwavering belief in self-determination, Harlem Labs isn’t just capturing culture—it is expanding the boundaries of what becomes possible when community becomes the canvas.
